source_title_hint: Finally Fix Your Tight Upper Traps (no stretching required)
primary_summary: Elevated shoulders are often caused by over‑active upper trapezius and tight rhomboids; pulling the shoulders back can worsen the issue. The root cause is limited rib‑cage expansion during inhalation, leading to compensatory activation of the upper traps. The video teaches a seated scapular‑separation drill using breath to open the space between the scapulae and spine, performed with low intensity and optional light band.

classification.usefulness_reason: Provides both an explanation of the biomechanical problem and a concrete corrective drill without requiring equipment

problem_statements: Elevated shoulders due to tight upper trapezius and rhomboids
Pull‑back shoulder exercises may increase upper trap activation
Limited rib‑cage expansion during inhalation reinforces tightness
key_visual_points: Gentle separation of shoulder blades away from the spine
Arms positioned at ~45° relative to trunk
exercises_mentioned: Seated scapular‑separation drill (optional light wrist band)
warnings_or_limitations: High‑intensity pulling exercises can worsen upper trap tightness

knowledge_units.title: Upper trap over‑activity causes shoulder elevation
knowledge_units.summary: When shoulders are elevated, the upper trapezius is often tight and over‑active, pulling the shoulders upward. The rhomboids also become tight because their fibers pull the scapulae upward‑diagonally.
observable_signs: Tension in the upper back and neck
mechanisms: Over‑active upper trap elevates the scapulae
Rhomboids' diagonal fiber orientation adds upward pull
when_useful: Explaining why pulling‑back exercises may feel uncomfortable

knowledge_units.title: Limited rib‑cage expansion reinforces trap tightness
knowledge_units.summary: Each inhalation should expand the rib cage circumferentially, especially the space between the scapulae and spine. Failure to do so leads to compensatory activation of the upper traps and neck muscles to elevate the rib cage.
observable_signs: Use of upper traps during inhalation
mechanisms: Insufficient thoracic expansion triggers compensatory muscle activation

knowledge_units.title: Seated scapular‑separation drill
knowledge_units.summary: Sit on a chair with sit bones evenly weighted, table height such that the forearms are at ~45° to the trunk. Optionally wrap a light band around the wrist. Gently pull the shoulder blades apart from the spine with very low intensity (1‑2/10).
execution_steps: Sit tall with sit bones evenly loaded
Place forearms at ~45° relative to trunk (using a table or desk for support)
Optional: wrap a very light band around the wrist
Very gently slide the shoulder blades away from the spine (scapular depression)
Keep intensity at 1‑2/10, focusing on breath‑driven expansion
cues: Breathe deeply to expand the rib cage
Feel the space opening between scapulae and spine
errors_to_avoid: Pulling too hard or using high intensity
when_useful: Improving scapular positioning for people with elevated shoulders
when_not_useful: During acute upper back injury where scapular movement is contraindicated
retest: Observe shoulder elevation at rest after 2‑3 weeks of practice
